summary.title: Write documentation first. Then build.
summary.one_liner: Writing out an idea as documentation or a press release before building clarifies what to build, guides development, and gives you docs at launch.
takeaways: Writing the idea down first (reference card, press release, memo) exposes gaps and sharpens the product before code is written.
A pre-written press release or packaging copy sets boundaries and a standard for when the product is ready to ship.
Keeping documentation alongside code helps the original developer and others understand why things were built as they were.
Rewriting and revising a document refines thinking, so writing and rewriting are part of the design process.
Amazon's use of narrative memos over slide decks is cited as an example of writing forcing better thought.
summary.summary: The article argues that writing the full idea out before building leads to better products. It supports this with historical examples: VisiCalc began as a reference card written by Dan Bricklin, Nest's features were judged against a press release by Tony Fadell, the Macintosh started as The Book of Macintosh, and Amazon uses narrative memos. It also cites Bezos's memo practice and Eugene Yan's remark about Amazon spending long periods on documents before coding. The piece is an opinion essay built on anecdotes and quotes rather than a how-to, and it ends with the advice to write, rewrite, and revise before building.
